content:
An NGO that raises money for individual patients or cases (a child's heart surgery, a cancer patient's chemotherapy, a family rebuilding after a fire) needs case pages that answer the question every donor silently asks: "Is this real, and will my money reach this person's treatment?" A good case page states who is being helped and why, in words and photos the patient or guardian has consented to; shows what the NGO has verified, such as hospital documents, an estimate and identity, without publishing the documents themselves; gives a specific target with a breakdown; explains where the money goes, usually to the hospital directly rather than to the family; and is updated until the case is closed, including what happens to any surplus. Behind the page sits a back office that records verification, consent, funds raised and fund use for every case. Getting this right is one of the most important parts of NGO website development in India for health and relief organisations, because the medical crowdfunding space has been damaged by fake campaigns and donors are rightly cautious.

This guide is for founders, programme heads and fundraising staff at hospitals' charitable trusts, patient-support NGOs, disaster-relief organisations and community foundations that run individual appeals, or want to move them from WhatsApp forwards to their own website.

## Why your own case pages, and not only a crowdfunding platform

Many NGOs list cases on large crowdfunding platforms, and there are good reasons to: built-in traffic, ready-made payment and verification flows, and a familiar interface for donors. There are also good reasons to run case pages on your own website, alone or alongside a platform:

- **Your organisation's credibility is the guarantee.** Donors giving through your site are trusting your NGO's verification and governance, which is the thing you are building over years.
- **The donor relationship stays with you.** You can thank donors, send updates and invite them to future appeals or monthly giving. On third-party platforms, access to donor contact details and communication is governed by the platform's terms.
- **Costs and timing are under your control.** Platform fees, payout timing and rules vary; your own pages run on your own payment arrangements.
- **You can connect cases to your programmes,** showing that individual appeals are part of a wider, accountable programme of work.

The trade-off is that you must provide the traffic, the verification process and the technology yourself. We compare these options in more depth in our guide to [your own website versus a crowdfunding platform](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-own-website-vs-crowdfunding-platform-2026).

## The trust problem you are designing for

Fake and exaggerated medical appeals are a known problem in India. Reporting by The News Minute, among others, has documented fraudulent campaigns and the damage they do to trust in genuine fundraising. Crowdfunding platforms publicly describe multi-step verification, including identity checks, hospital document verification and confirming the treatment with the hospital, before a campaign goes live.

Your case pages have to show, quickly and visibly, that your NGO does at least this much, and that the money is controlled. Donors will not read your verification policy unless the page makes it easy to understand at a glance.

## Building the verification process first

The website cannot be more trustworthy than the process behind it. Before designing pages, agree a written verification procedure. A typical one covers:

### Identity and relationship

- Identity of the patient and of the guardian or family member who requested help.
- Proof of relationship where a guardian or relative is acting for the patient.
- Contact details checked by a call or visit.

### Medical need

- A diagnosis or medical summary from the treating doctor or hospital.
- A cost estimate on hospital letterhead, with the hospital's contact details.
- Confirmation by the NGO directly with the hospital (a call to the billing or social work department, not to a number supplied by the family) that the patient is under treatment and the estimate is genuine.

### Financial need

- What the family can contribute, insurance cover and any government scheme eligibility checked.
- Other appeals running for the same patient elsewhere, which you should know about before you launch yours.

### Sign-off

- Named staff member who verified each item, with dates.
- Approval by a second person, such as a programme head, before publication.

Keep all of this in your back office, not on the public page. The page should summarise what was checked; the documents stay private.

## What a case page should contain

### 1. A clear, respectful summary at the top

Within the first screen, the donor should see:

- The patient's first name or chosen name (or a pseudonym, with a note saying so), approximate age and city or district.
- The condition and treatment in plain language: "needs open-heart surgery to repair a hole in the heart" rather than only a medical term.
- The hospital name, if the hospital and family agree.
- Amount needed, amount raised so far and the deadline linked to the treatment date.
- A clear "Donate" button.

Avoid sensational headlines and graphic images. Dignified, factual appeals build longer-term trust, and many donors find exploitative imagery off-putting.

### 2. A "Verified by [NGO name]" panel

A short, visible panel listing what your team checked:

- Medical documents reviewed: yes, date
- Treatment and estimate confirmed with hospital: yes, date
- Identity and relationship verified: yes
- Verified by: role of the staff member, such as "Programme Officer, Medical Aid"

Do not publish the actual documents, Aadhaar numbers, full addresses or hospital registration numbers. A redacted image of an estimate is sometimes used to reassure donors, but consider whether it adds enough to justify the privacy risk. In most cases, a clear statement of what was verified, backed by your NGO's reputation and contact details, is better.

### 3. The story, told with consent

Explain briefly who the patient is, what happened, what the treatment will achieve and why the family needs help. Use the family's own words where possible, with their approval of the final text. Our guide to [beneficiary stories, photos and consent](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-beneficiary-stories-photos-consent-2026) covers how to collect and record consent for stories and photos.

### 4. The cost breakdown

Show how the target was calculated:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Surgery and hospital stay (hospital estimate) | ₹X |
| Medicines and follow-up for three months | ₹Y |
| Less: family contribution / insurance / scheme | −₹Z |
| **Amount to be raised** | **₹T** |

The figures above are placeholders for illustration. A breakdown shows donors that the target is grounded in a real estimate and not rounded up.

### 5. Where the money goes

State plainly how funds are used. The most trust-building approach, used by many NGOs, is that funds are paid by the NGO directly to the hospital against bills, not handed to the family in cash. Say that on the page. If some funds go to the family for travel or living costs during treatment, say so and explain how that is controlled.

### 6. What happens if the target is exceeded or the treatment changes

This is the section most case pages leave out, and the one that causes the most disputes. Before launching, decide and publish a policy covering:

- **Over-funding:** for example, surplus is used for the patient's follow-up care, or transferred to your general medical aid fund to help other patients.
- **Treatment cancelled or the patient passes away:** for example, funds already paid to the hospital are not recoverable, and any balance goes to the medical aid fund.
- **Treatment cost rises:** for example, the target may be increased with an update explaining why.

Link to the full policy from every case page and from the donation form. Donors who know the rules in advance rarely complain when they are applied.

### 7. Updates until the case is closed

Every case page needs a dated updates section:

- Surgery done, patient recovering
- Bills paid to the hospital, amount
- Patient discharged
- Case closed, with final amounts raised and used

A case page that stops updating the day the target is reached looks like a scam, even when it is not. Plan updates as part of the case workflow, and send them to donors by email or WhatsApp as well as posting them on the page.

### 8. Contact and reporting

Show a named contact (role, email, phone) for questions about the case, and a way to report a concern. A visible "Report a concern about this appeal" link signals that you take misuse seriously.

## Consent and privacy: the part that is easiest to get wrong

Medical information is among the most sensitive information an NGO handles. Even where the law does not use the word "sensitive", donors, families and regulators expect it to be handled with great care.

### Written, specific consent

Get written consent from the patient, or from a parent or lawful guardian if the patient is a child or cannot consent, covering:

- Exactly what will be published: name or pseudonym, age, location, condition, hospital, photos, video.
- Where it will be published: website, social media, WhatsApp, email, print.
- How long it will remain online, and that they can ask for it to be taken down or anonymised.
- That they have seen and approved the final story.

Record the consent with the case in your back office, with the date and version of the text approved.

### Children's data

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires verifiable consent of a parent or lawful guardian before processing a child's personal data, and the DPDP Rules notified in November 2025 set out how that consent is to be obtained, with most operational provisions coming into force after an eighteen-month transition. Many medical appeals are for children, so design your consent process around a parent or guardian from the start, and have your forms reviewed by a lawyer familiar with the Act.

### Minimise what you publish

- Use first names or pseudonyms where possible.
- Do not publish exact addresses, school names, Aadhaar or other identity numbers, or full hospital file numbers.
- Choose photos that show the person with dignity, not in distress, and avoid images that reveal medical details the family has not agreed to share.
- Remove or anonymise the page after the agreed period, keeping the financial record internally.

### Secure the back office

Verification documents, consent forms and hospital bills should be stored in a system with role-based access, not in shared drives or personal WhatsApp chats. Limit who can view documents, keep an access log if possible, and delete documents you no longer need according to a retention schedule.

## The back office behind the pages

Case pages work only if staff can create, verify, publish, update and close cases without a developer. A case management system, whether a module of your donation platform, a custom build or a configured CRM, typically needs:

- **Case records** with status: submitted, under verification, approved, live, target reached, funds disbursed, closed.
- **Verification checklist** with document uploads, named verifier and approval step.
- **Consent records** linked to each case.
- **Funds tracking:** amount raised online and offline, payments made to the hospital, balance.
- **Updates** written once and published to the page and sent to that case's donors.
- **Roles:** field staff can submit cases, programme heads approve, communications staff edit the public text, finance records disbursements.
- **Reports** for trustees, auditors and donors.

Case creation portals are among the NGO systems we build, either alongside our Give Setu donation platform or as custom workflows for organisations with specific needs. Whatever system you use, insist that a case cannot go live until verification and consent are recorded.

## Donation flow details for case appeals

### Linking each donation to the case

Every donation from a case page must be recorded against that case, so totals and progress bars are accurate and so you can update and thank the right donors. Test this with online donations and with offline ones entered by staff.

### Progress and deadlines

Progress bars motivate giving when they are accurate. Update them automatically from your donation records, include offline gifts once received, and stop accepting donations for a case when it closes, redirecting visitors to your general medical aid fund or to other open cases. Our guide to [fundraising progress bars and goal thermometers](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-fundraising-progress-bar-goal-thermometer-2026) covers accuracy and design.

### Receipts and thank-you

Send an immediate thank-you naming the case, and tell donors they will receive updates. Make sure your receipts reflect the correct legal donee, which is your NGO, not the patient.

### Social sharing

Most case appeals spread on WhatsApp. Set up sharing previews (title, image and description) that respect the consent agreed, and use tracked links so you can see which channels bring donations.

## A listing page for open cases

If you run several appeals at once, a listing page lets donors choose:

- Show only live, verified cases, with a short summary, progress and deadline.
- Include filters by condition type or location only if you have enough cases to need them.
- Add a "Give where most needed" option to your general medical aid fund, which helps patients who are less photogenic or whose stories are harder to tell.
- Keep a section of closed cases with outcomes, which is strong evidence that your process works.

## Common mistakes on NGO case pages

- **Publishing medical reports and identity documents** in full to "prove" a case.
- **No policy for surplus funds,** leading to disputes when an appeal over-raises.
- **No updates** after the target is reached.
- **Appeals created directly by staff on social media** without going through verification.
- **Photos used without written consent,** or used long after the agreed period.
- **Donations not linked to the case,** so progress bars are wrong and donors cannot be updated.
- **Case pages left open after the patient has been treated,** still collecting money.

## Timeline and budget ranges

For an NGO that already has a donation website, adding case pages with a simple back office (case records, verification checklist, consent upload, case-linked donations and updates) typically takes four to ten weeks, depending on the platform and how much reporting is needed. A full case management system with roles, approvals, disbursement tracking and donor update automation is a larger project. ## Frequently asked questions

### How can donors know a medical fundraising appeal is genuine?

Look for a named, registered organisation with contact details, a clear statement of what was verified (hospital documents, treatment confirmed with the hospital, identity), a cost breakdown, a statement that funds are paid to the hospital, and regular dated updates. NGOs should make all of this visible on every case page.

### Should an NGO publish patients' medical documents on its website?

No. Publishing full medical reports, identity documents or addresses creates privacy risks for the patient. Verify documents privately, keep them in a secure back office, and show donors a summary of what was checked, by whom and when.

### What should happen to extra money raised for a patient?

The NGO should decide and publish its policy before the appeal goes live. Common approaches are to use surplus for the patient's follow-up care or to transfer it to a general medical aid fund for other patients. Link the policy from every case page and the donation form.

### Do we need consent to share a patient's story and photos?

Yes. Get written consent from the patient, or a parent or guardian for a child, covering exactly what will be published, where and for how long, and let them approve the final text. India's DPDP Act requires verifiable parental consent for processing children's personal data.

### Can an NGO raise funds for individual patients on its own website?

Yes, many do, alongside or instead of crowdfunding platforms. It requires a written verification process, consent records, case-linked donation tracking, a clear fund-use policy and regular updates. Your own pages keep the donor relationship with your NGO.
